reading.body:
Data center operators in small European towns often remain unidentified in public records, making their role in regional compute infrastructure invisible.

This facility in Dueville, Italy appears on OpenStreetMap as a data center but carries only the generic name "Set," which yields no company identity. The research exhausted available search capacity without confirming the operator, the facility's purpose, or its capacity. Dueville sits in the Veneto region near Vicenza, an area with mixed light industrial and small technology businesses, but nothing in the data distinguishes this site as serving AI workloads or regional compute needs.

The incompleteness here is the point. A facility tagged as telecom infrastructure exists in the landscape but remains functionally anonymous to external observers. Without operator identity, construction date, power capacity, or cooling infrastructure, no reader can assess whether this contributes meaningfully to compute availability in northern Italy or serves only local connectivity. The data does not cover what "Set" actually does or how much power it draws.

This illustrates a broader problem for mapping compute's infrastructure base: many small or regional data centers never achieve public documentation thorough enough to answer basic questions about their role in the power grid or AI scaling constraints.
